extracted.intended_audience: academic researchers, postdocs, grad students and readers of science-policy/academia blogs
extracted.subtask_description: A multi-topic academic blog post (DrugMonkey) containing commentary on authorship practices, citation phrasing, and a year‑end blogging meme. The page mixes informal opinion with short prescriptive statements about how to cite and attribute authorship and how to participate in a blog meme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation phrasing per journal style guide
rubrics_metrics.description: There are style guides for journals as to how previous studies are to be cited and how they are to be referred to in the text. One typical style guide might suggest that you use 'As shown by Gun et al (2009), the PhysioWhimple nucleus is critical in…'. You might also resort to the more conversational 'Gun and colleagues demonstrated…'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the journal's style guide for in-text citation phrasing; acceptable alternatives include either the parenthetical 'As shown by X et al (Year)…' or the narrative 'X and colleagues demonstrated…' depending on tone and journal conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing papers with co-equal contributors (include co-equal names)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the paper in question indicates co-equal contribution, then you should say 'Genedog, Tideliar and colleagues showed….'. Right? You should absolutely insist on including the name of the co-equal authors, should you not? Especially if you are one of those who insists that this designation is meaningful…
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a paper designates specific authors as co-equal contributors, name those authors in your citation (e.g., 'A, B and colleagues') rather than anonymizing or omitting them; this preserves the intended attribution when the co-equal designation is considered meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of co-equal contribution designations in author lists
rubrics_metrics.description: Example criticized: 'EIGHT authors who…. D.S., A.B., M. Maroteaux, T.J., C.P.M., R.S., J.-A.G., and G.S. contributed equally to this work.' The post notes: 'To make it extra hilarious please note that the first four are listed first authors and the last four are…listed last authors. This is ridiculous.' Going by affiliations it looks like typical trainee-PI pairings, so it would make more sense to identify the four trainees and the four PIs as contributing equally compared with each other—but not across the trainee/PI divide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'contributed equally' designations sensibly: avoid blanket equality claims that span clearly different roles (e.g., trainees vs PIs). If equality is claimed, the grouping should reflect comparable contributions (e.g., trainees equal to trainees; PIs equal to PIs) rather than asserting equivalence across hierarchical or role-based divides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blog year‑end meme rule: post first-sentence per month
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules for this blog meme are quite simple. -Post the link and first sentence from the first blog entry for each month of the past year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For the 'Twelve Months' blog meme, collect for each month of the year: (1) a link to the month's first blog entry and (2) the first sentence from that entry. This is the complete participation requirement for the meme.
